newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy '98 budget to lop spending, raise tax - papers.
newsitem.headline: Italy '98 budget to lop spending, raise tax - papers.

text.p: Italy plans some 17 trillion lire of ($10 billion) state spending cuts next year in its efforts to trim its budget deficit and convince its EU partners it is fit to join a single currency, newspapers said on Saturday.

La Repubblica said the budget, which is expected to total 25.5 trillion in deficit-trimming measures, would contain 17 trillion lire of spending cuts, including 7.0 to 8.0 trillion lire in reforms to welfare spending.
On the other side, "a substantial part of the 1998 measures will be through new taxes," the newspaper said, citing the budget ministry as its source.

Financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said the government aimed to boost income by 8.0 trillion lire via changes to valued added tax (VAT) and other revenue raising measures, make 8.0 trillion lire in welfare cuts and find the rest from "assorted cuts".

According to a government official, the ruling centre-left coalition is planning a 1998 budget which will cut a total 25.5 trillion lire from the deficit and hold its ratio with Italy's gross domestic product (GDP) below the three percent level required to take part in economic and monetary union (EMU).
Budget under-secretary Giorgio Macciotta told Reuters on Friday the deficit-GDP ratio was heading for 4.0 percent in 1998 and needed to narrow by 1.2 percent or 25 trillion lire.
The 1998 budget will be outlined in the annual document of three year rolling economic targets (DPEF) which Prime Minister Romano Prodi's cabinet is due to discuss next week.

Prodi is determined Italy will rank among the first nations forming EMU at its expected start in 1999. He has already taken budget deficit cutting measures of 78 trillion lire in the last six months to force the deficit down to three percent of GDP by year-end -- a prerequisite for joining the single currency.
But economists and some of Italy's EU partners doubt the steps taken are sustainable into 1998 and the EU Commission warned recently Italy's deficit is likely to blow out to 3.9 percent in 1998.
La Repubblica said VAT hikes would probably bring three to four trillion lire into state coffers.

Il Sole said the amount would be closer to 5.2 trillion and the change could be adopted as early as October in legislation tied to the 1998 budget law. The draft budget law must be presented to parliament by the end of September.

Further revenue would come from higher levies on petrol, and utility tariffs, with 700 billion from a programme to beat tax evasion, 1.7 trillion from sales of fixed assets and 850 billion from changes in transfers to local authorities.
Il Sole said the government still had to find another three trillion lire or so but said a controversial 'Euro tax' imposed this year would not be replaced by other taxes.

On spending, Il Sole broke the eight trillion welfare figure into 5.2 trillion in state pensions through altering retirement ages and speeding up reforms made by the previous government, as well health and social security sector cuts.

Some 3.7 trillion would come from public administration reforms, 1.2 trillion in savings by government ministries and two trillion from cuts in spending in the rail, post and higher education sectors.

Il Sole said the DPEF would indicate a 1998 budget at around 25 trillion lire but total measures for 1998 would reach 28 trillion, with the extra three trillion included in an additional measure to accompany the 1998 budget law.
It also said servicing Italy's debt in 1998 was estimated at 165 trillion lire, down from 187 trillion forecast for 1997. ($1=1,672 lire)
